metadata.title: Electrochemical sensing of cell viability: A scalable platform from 2D monolayers to 3D tissue models

sources.label: Summary
sources.text:
Summary

The trend toward animal-free testing in toxicology and drug development has accelerated the adoption of complex 3D in vitro models. However, standard colorimetric viability assays suffer from severe limitations due to chemical interferences. To address these challenges, we designed a versatile sensor platform based on screen-printed carbon electrodes to overcome optical bottlenecks by quantifying cell viability through the electrochemical reduction of MTS-formazan. The electrochemical sensor was validated in 2D human dermal fibroblasts and keratinocytes at different cell confluences. Importantly, it successfully assessed viability in both 2D cell monolayer cultures and reconstructed human epidermis exposed to an OECD-panel of irritant and non-irritant chemicals. The electrochemical approach provides a technologically robust and interference-free tool that enhances reliability in viability assays, overcoming the traditional limitations of colorimetric measurements. This methodology represents a transversal tool applicable to any tissue offering a robust and promising solution for high-throughput screening in pharmacology, cosmetics, and biomedical research.

Keywords: electrochemical sensor, MTS, cell confluence, cell viability, 2D cell cultures, 3D in vitro tissue models, cyclovoltammetry

sources.label: Introduction
sources.text:
Introduction

The path that a new drug candidate must follow to reach the market is a complex, multi-stage process that starts with the initial drug discovery, is followed by preclinical testing and finishes with an extensive clinical trial. Traditionally, the preclinical phase has served as the critical phase to test safety and efficacy, relying heavily on animal models to predict human response before going to the clinical stages.1,2,3 However, this traditional pipeline is facing significant ethical and economic transformation due to lower efficiency rates—where drugs successful in animals fail in humans—and growing regulatory pressure. A global paradigm shift is also driven by strict international frameworks restricting animal use. Landmark initiatives such as the EU Cosmetics Regulation (EC 1223/2009), the REACH Regulation (EC 1907/2006) for chemical safety, and the FDA Modernization Act 2.0 in the United States4,5 have set a worldwide precedent to minimize animal testing. Consequently, there is an urgent demand across the scientific community, as well as with pharmaceutical, chemical, and cosmetic industries for reliable, ethically approved in vitro methodologies capable of replacing animal models while ensuring robust safety standards.

To meet these demands, the field has moved beyond simplistic 2D cell monolayers, which often lack the physiological complexity required for accurate toxicity prediction. The industry standard is shifting toward 3D in vitro models, such as organoids, spheroids, and reconstructed tissues (cornea, skin, oral, airway, alveolar, kidney, liver, or intestine).6,7 These models have become indispensable tools, some of them even being validated by the OECD for regulatory decision-making.8 More specifically, reconstructed human epidermis (RHE) models, which are composed of differentiated keratinocyte layers, are relevant in vitro systems able to mimic the stratum corneum and barrier functions of real skin.9 These systems are valuable in vitro tools that offer ethical and physiologically relevant alternatives to animal models for chemical testing, drug permeation, and disease modeling. However, while the biological models have evolved significantly to mimic human physiology, the analytical techniques used to monitor them have lagged behind.

Currently, the assessment of cell viability in these tissues relies predominantly on colorimetric assays that measure metabolic activity, such as the reduction of the 3-(4,5-dimethylthiazol-2-yl)-2,5-diphenyltetrazolium bromide (MTT) to formazan salt. Mitochondrial NADH is the primary electron donor in enzymatic reactions that reduce the yellow MTT tetrazolium salt into purple formazan crystals.10 Then, the amount of reduced product is measured using a spectrophotometer. MTT provides a reliable and standardized method, as it is internationally accepted for assessing cell viability, as well as a chemical classification method for irritation and corrosion exposure. However, it also presents several limitations when used in toxicity studies, such as possible interference with some chemicals leading to false positives, non-specific absorption, incomplete penetration in 3D models, or low chemical solubility.11,12,13,14,15,16 Furthermore, MTT can exhibit cytotoxicity due to the formation of insoluble formazan crystals within the cells, potentially altering cellular metabolism and leading to inaccurate viability measurements.11

To overcome some of these limitations, the MTS assay was developed as a second-generation tetrazolium assay. The electrochemical quantification of cell viability is based on the reduction of the tetrazolium salt MTS [3-(4,5-dimethylthiazol-2-yl)-5-(3-carboxymethoxyphenyl)-2-(4-sulfophenyl)-2H-tetrazolium] into its soluble formazan derivative (Figure S1). This process occurs via a two-electron reduction mechanism.17,18 Unlike MTT, the MTS reagent directly produces a soluble formazan product, eliminating the need for solubilization steps and thereby reducing overall assay time, complexity, and accuracy. MTS has been used in several in vitro applications and for a wide range of cell types and organs. For instance, it has been effectively used in assessing the survival fraction of irradiated colon cancer cells,17 determining the cytotoxicity of contact lens care products on human corneal epithelial cells,19,20 and evaluating the effects of various compounds or devices on human dermal fibroblasts, keratinocytes,21 and RHE.22,23 However, regardless of these results, the deficiencies of the colorimetric technique commonly used in MTS assays for cell viability has led to the OECD’s reluctance to accept this method due to susceptibility to interference.

Beyond conventional spectrophotometric techniques, electrochemical biosensors have emerged as powerful tools, for instance, in a wide range of tissue engineering applications due to their high sensitivity, rapid response, miniaturization potential, and direct electrical readout.24 These platforms offer significant advantages (Table S1) for detecting a wide range of biomarkers and physiological changes.25 For instance, electrochemical sensors have been developed for the non-invasive detection of skin analytes such as glucose,26 lactate,27 and pH28 for continuous health monitoring or diagnostics. In the context of cytotoxicity and in vitro tissue engineering, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) has been extensively used to monitor cell adhesion, proliferation, and barrier integrity in real-time, providing valuable insights into cellular health and tissue development.29,30,31 Furthermore, enzyme-based electrochemical biosensors have been applied to detect specific enzymes or metabolites indicative of cellular stress or damage in cell cultures.32,33 While these studies highlight the versatility of electrochemical sensing in cell-based assays and tissue engineering research, they still lack robust, interference-free, and high-throughput performance, especially for standardized cell viability endpoint studies in complex 3D human tissue models.

To address these limitations and exploit the inherent advantages of electrochemical detection, we developed a groundbreaking electrochemical sensor platform for the direct and accurate measurement of cell viability, taking advantage of the inherent capabilities of electrochemical detection. This sensor aimed to measure the reduction of MTS to formazan more accurately than spectrophotometry techniques. Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NADH), a physiologically relevant reducing agent,18 was used to validate the sensor, and further biological analyses were performed inhibiting its action with NADH-oxidase, in order to validate the reducing power to formazan.34 The electrochemical sensor has demonstrated its ability to quantify cell confluence and cell viability in human skin fibroblasts and keratinocytes. The proposed method is described as a “scalable platform” due to its inherent compatibility with high-throughput architectures. This scalability ensures that the transition from bench-top proof-of-concept to automated industrial toxicity screening is technically straightforward, maintaining analytical performance while significantly increasing sample throughput. To demonstrate the broad applicability of this technology, we validated the sensor using RHE as a proof-of-concept model. We compared our electrochemical sensor against standard spectrophotometry under OECD TG 439 irritation protocols using a panel of reference chemicals. This approach effectively decouples the viability signal from optical constraints: it translates the metabolic reduction of MTS into a precise electric current rather than a color change. This method eliminates the need for crystal solubilization, avoids optical interference from the tissue or medium, and offers a straightforward path toward automation and high-throughput screening. While spectrophotometric MTS assays are prone to inaccuracies due to light scattering by tissue debris and optical interference from colored or turbid chemicals,35 the proposed electrochemical detection cuts out these issues by taking advantage of the specific redox window of formazan, which remains independent of the sample’s optical properties. The successful validation in this complex skin model serves as a robust demonstration of its potential as reproducible, non-destructive, and quantitative high-throughput system that can be applicable to any tissue model, enabling more accurate, automated, and animal-free drug development pipelines.

sources.label: Results
sources.text:
Results

To address the limitations of conventional colorimetric assays for cell viability assessment, an alternative electrochemical method utilizing screen-printed carbon electrodes (SPCEs) was developed for the measurement of MTS reduction. The reduction of the MTS tetrazolium salt into its formazan derivative involves a two-electron/two-proton transfer that results in the opening of the tetrazole ring. This chemical transformation, thoroughly described in previous studies18,36 is the basis for both the optical change and the electrochemical signal reported here. The feasibility of this approach primarily depends on two critical aspects: first, the absence of interfering electrochemical signals from the cell culture media components, and second, the electrochemical detectability of the reduced MTS molecule signal.

sources.label: Electrochemical characterization of MTS reduction and culture media interference
sources.text:
Electrochemical characterization of MTS reduction and culture media interference

This initial section focuses on the study of the electrochemical background of commonly used biological media. For that purpose, cyclic voltammetry (CV) was employed to characterize the electrochemical response of the individual components of the cell culture environment, namely, DMEM and EpiLife medium,37 that is used for culturing N/TERT-1 and hDFs, respectively. As shown in Figure 1, no significant oxidation or reduction peaks were observed across the scanned potential range of −0.6 V to +0.7 V for any of the tested media. The absence of characteristic current responses within this electrochemical window confirms that these media components do not exhibit intrinsic electroactivity under the experimental conditions, thereby ensuring minimal interference with the subsequent detection of the MTS reduction product. This initial experiment is crucial for validating the specificity of the electrochemical sensor for MTS.

After the confirmation of electrochemical inactivity of the culture media, the electrochemical reduction of MTS mediated by NADH38 was investigated using CV (Figure 2). NADH18 was employed as a model reducing agent to simulate the cellular metabolic activity that would typically convert MTS to its formazan product. The sensing principle relies on the mechanism where metabolically active cells produce NADH, which reduces the MTS inner salt into a soluble formazan product. This formazan is the primary electroactive analyte in our system. During the CV scan, the formazan undergoes a 2-electron reduction at the working electrode, generating a cathodic peak between −0.2 and −0.1 V. Therefore, the peak current is directly proportional to the formazan concentration, which in turn reflects the amount of NADH produced by the cells.39

As shown in Figure 2A, the CV obtained from MTS solutions reduced by varying concentrations of NADH revealed a characteristic negative current peak in the cathodic scan, specifically within the potential range of −0.3 to −0.1 V (highlighted by the red square). This peak corresponds to the electrochemical oxidation of the NADH-reduced formazan product of MTS. A more detailed examination of this region (Figure 2B) demonstrates a clear correlation between the NADH concentration and the magnitude of this reduction peak. Specifically, as the concentration of NADH increased from 0.01 to 0.1 mg/mL, a corresponding increase in the absolute magnitude of the current peak was observed, indicating a stronger electrochemical signal with higher concentrations of reduced MTS.

The linear relationship between NADH concentration and MTS reduction was quantitatively obtained using both the conventional spectrophotometric method and the proposed electrochemical sensor, in the presence of EpiLife and DMEM culture media. As demonstrated in Figure 3, increasing concentrations of NADH (0.005–0.1 mg/mL) led to a proportional increase in MTS reduction.

For the conventional spectrophotometric method, a strong linear regression was observed between NADH concentration and mean absorbance for both EpiLife (Figure 3A, R2 = 0.9522) and DMEM (Figure 3C, R2 = 0.9486). Similarly, the electrochemical sensor exhibited excellent linearity, with the current intensity peak showing a strong linear correlation with NADH concentration in EpiLife (Figure 3B, R2 = 0.9493) and DMEM (Figure 3D, R2 = 0.9667).

Moreover, the sensor displayed a linear response with a calculated limit of detection (LOD) calculated based on the linear regression data from our CV measurements40 and yielding a value of 0.0047 mg/mL. By using the standard deviation of the residuals (Sy.x = 0.2292) and the slope from this linear fit, we determined an LOD of practical sensitivity of our CV-based method. This level of sensitivity (Figure S3) demonstrates its suitability for quantitative cell viability monitoring in both 2D monolayers and complex 3D tissue models, where formazan production typically exceeds this threshold. The analytical performance of the sensor was further validated using differential pulse voltammetry (DPV), showing high sensitivity even at low NADH concentrations (Figure S4) and supporting the analytical performance of the proposed sensor.41

Furthermore, a critical aspect for validation of the proposed electrochemical method was to establish its correlation with the established spectrophotometric assay. Direct comparison of the data obtained from both methods revealed a strong linear correlation between the electrochemical current intensity and the spectrophotometric absorbance values. This was clearly shown in both EpiLife (Figure 3E, R2 = 0.9327) and DMEM (Figure 3F, R2 = 0.9023). The high R2 values demonstrate that the electrochemical sensor provides results that are highly consistent with the gold standard colorimetric assay, reinforcing its potential as a reliable alternative for MTS reduction measurements.

To ensure that the measured current peak originates exclusively from the MTS-reduction product (formazan), several control experiments were conducted. As shown in Figure S2, no electrochemical activity was observed for the culture medium alone or for the individual components (MTS or NADH) within the scanned potential range. The characteristic reduction peak only emerged upon the combination of all reagents, confirming the selectivity of the platform for formazan quantification.

To evaluate the precision and reproducibility of the developed electrochemical sensor compared to the conventional spectrophotometric method, the percentage error in the measurements of MTS reduction was quantified. As shown in Figure 4, the electrochemical readings consistently exhibited improved precision. Statistical analysis revealed significant differences in the variability of results between the two methods (p < 0.01).

Specifically, for measurements conducted in EpiLife medium, the electrochemical sensor yielded a mean percentage error of 1.73 ± 1.19% for the current intensity readings. In contrast, the spectrophotometric measurements in EpiLife showed a higher mean percentage error of 4.62 ± 3.09%. Similarly, when evaluated in DMEM, the electrochemical method demonstrated a mean error of 2.63 ± 1.64%, which was remarkably lower than the 5.25 ± 3.44% observed for the absorbance readings. The consistently smaller standard deviations and less dispersed data points associated with the electrochemical measurements (Figure 4) underscore higher consistency and precision.

sources.label: Cell confluency and MTS electrochemical signal correlation
sources.text:
Cell confluency and MTS electrochemical signal correlation

Following the initial validation of the electrochemical sensor and its correlation with the spectrophotometric method in cell-free systems, the applicability of the sensor to measure cell metabolic activity was investigated using varying cell confluency. This experiment aimed to confirm that the presence of cells, and their metabolic state, would not introduce interfering signals and that the established correlation between the two detection methods would be maintained in a biological context.

hDFs were seeded at different confluency percentages (10%–100%), and MTS reduction was subsequently measured using both the conventional spectrophotometric assay and the proposed electrochemical sensor. As presented in Figure 5, a strong linear correlation was observed between cell confluency and MTS reduction for both measurement techniques. The mean absorbance (OD) measured by spectrophotometry showed a good linear relationship with cell confluency (Figure 5A, R2 = 0.9684). Similarly, the electrochemical current intensity peak also demonstrated linearity with cell confluency (Figure 5B, R2 = 0.9358). These results confirm the ability of the sensor to quantitatively detect cellular metabolic activity and directly correlate it with cell density.

Moreover, the strong correlation between the two measurement methods was maintained in the presence of living cells. A robust linear relationship was observed when comparing the electrochemical current intensity readings directly against the spectrophotometric absorbance values (Figure 5C, R2 = 0.9056). This high coefficient of determination indicates that the electrochemical sensor provides an equivalent and reliable readout of MTS reduction in a cellular environment.

To further demonstrate the causal link between cellular metabolism and the electrochemical response, a validation assay using a NADH production inhibitor was performed. As shown in Figures 5C and 5D, cells treated with NADH-oxidase exhibited a significant decrease in the reduction peak current compared to the positive control. To identify any potential artifacts caused by the solvent, a control with DMSO was included at the same concentration used in the inhibitor treatment, showing no significant impact on the signal. These results confirm that the electrochemical readout is directly dependent on the enzymatic reduction of MTS via cellular NADH-oxidase, reinforcing the mechanistic validity of our platform as previously suggested by similar mitochondrial inhibition studies.34

sources.label: Cell monolayer viability after chemical exposure
sources.text:
Cell monolayer viability after chemical exposure

A crucial application for the proposed biosensor in skin irritation assessment is its ability to accurately determine cell viability following chemical exposure. This experiment aimed to validate the proposed electrochemical method as a reliable procedure for chemical toxicity determination, aligning with established guidelines for assessing adverse outcomes such as tissue damage. Chemicals utilized in this study were selected based on their GHS classifications: 5% KOH and 1-decanol are categorized as irritants (Category 2), while isopropanol and 1-bromo-4-chlorobutane are classified as “No Category” (non-irritants). PBS served as negative control and 5% SDS as positive control.

MTS reduction measurements, obtained from both the electrochemical sensor and the conventional spectrophotometric method, showed consistent trends in both primary hDFs and immortalized N/TERT-1 human keratinocytes after 3-min chemical exposure and a 15-min recovery period. As shown in Figure 6, both methods clearly demonstrated a significant reduction in MTS signal for the known irritants (SDS 5% aq., KOH 5% aq., and 1-decanol), indicating cell damage. On the contrary, the “No Category” chemicals (isopropanol, 1-bromo-4-chlorobutane) generally showed higher MTS signals, reflecting less cellular toxicity. These preliminary trends indicate qualitative agreement between the two methods, identifying the toxic potential of the tested chemicals.

Cell viability percentages were subsequently calculated by normalizing the MTS reduction signals to the negative control (PBS), which was set as 100% viability, and the positive control (SDS 5% aq.) as 0% viability. A direct comparison of the calculated viabilities (Figure 7) revealed no statistically significant differences between the electrochemical and spectrophotometric methods for most chemicals and cell lines. The only exception was observed for 5% KOH exposure in hDFs, where a statistically significant difference was found between the two methods (p < 0.01).

sources.label: RHE viability after chemical exposure
sources.text:
RHE viability after chemical exposure

To further validate the clinical and regulatory relevance of the electrochemical sensor for skin toxicity assessment, its performance was evaluated using RHE models. RHE models are advanced in vitro tissue constructs that closely mimic the physiological and morphological characteristics of human skin, making them highly valuable alternatives to animal testing for irritation and corrosion studies.42

As demonstrated in Figure 8, both the electrochemical sensor and the conventional spectrophotometric method consistently detected changes in RHE viability after exposure to various chemicals. Similar to the monolayer cell cultures, RHE viability was calculated relative to the negative control (PBS), set as 100%. The positive control, 5% aqueous SDS, induced near-complete cell death, with both methods showing viability close to 0%.

For irritant chemicals such as 5% KOH, HCl, 1-decanol, and sulfuric acid, both detection methods indicated a significant reduction in RHE viability compared to the negative control. In contrast, chemicals previously classified as “No Category” or milder irritants, such as 1-bromo-4-chlorobutane, and isopropanol, generally showed higher residual viability, indicating their reduced toxic potential to the RHE model43 and in agreement with test guidelines.

Crucially, a direct comparison of the viability percentages obtained by the electrochemical and spectrophotometric methods for RHE models revealed a high degree of agreement. For all tested chemicals, no statistically significant differences were observed between the two measurzement approaches (p < 0.001 for SDS 5% aq., and no significance for the others).

While the inherent biological variability of the RHE models increased the standard deviation in both methods (Figures 5, 6, and 7), the electrochemical sensor consistently provided a robust correlation with the cell viability state, matching the reliability of the traditional spectrophotometric assay while offering the advantage of being non-destructive.

sources.label: Discussion
sources.text:
Discussion

The development of reliable analytical tools for complex in vitro models requires overcoming the limitations of traditional optical assays. The results presented in this study demonstrate that the proposed electrochemical platform successfully decouples viability measurements from optical constraints.

A significant advantage of the developed electrochemical sensor is its ability to eliminate potential interferences arising from cell culture media components, such as DMEM or EpiLife, confirming that, unlike conventional colorimetric assays, which can be susceptible to background absorbance from colored media,13 this methodology shows a clear stability across various culture media tested.

The strong linear correlation observed between NADH concentration, and the electrochemical signal (R2 > 0.90) validates the sensor’s ability to quantitatively monitor metabolic fluctuations. The precise and sensitive detection of this negative peak current provides a robust and direct measure of reducing equivalents, establishing the basis for accurate cell viability assessment in subsequent biological applications, surpassing the limitations often associated with traditional colorimetric methods.44 The high coefficients of determination (R2 > 0.90 for both EpiLife and DMEM) confirm the robust dependence response of MTS reduction to NADH concentration for both measurement techniques, thus highlighting the sensitivity and reliability of the electrochemical approach.18,45 Unlike traditional spectrophotometric assays that can be limited by chemical interference or optical interferences and path-length dependency due to the Beer-Lambert Law,35 the proposed electrochemical platform relies on surface-area-dependent redox reactions. This approach provides a clear quantitative readout with a sensitivity (LOD: 0.0046 mg/mL) that matches the requirements for high-throughput screening in bioengineering applications.

The strong reduction in measurement variability is essential for ensuring the reliability of results and enhancing confidence in subsequent cell metabolic activity measurements. These findings collectively highlight enhanced reliability and precision of the electrochemical method for MTS reduction assessment across different relevant biological media.11,46

Importantly, this correlation held true in biological environments containing living cells (hDFs), as evidenced by the linearity with cell confluency. While cells are known to secrete various biomolecules, including growth factors, hormones, and soluble signaling molecules,47 which could potentially interfere with electrochemical measurements, these results demonstrated no apparent disturbance in the sensor’s readings. However, the ability to distinguish between varying cell densities with high precision further reinforces the specificity and robustness of the electrochemical method for monitoring cell proliferation dynamics in real-time.

While validated here using skin-derived cells, fibroblasts and keratinocytes, the underlying principle of the sensor is universal to mammalian metabolism. The results indicated that the electrochemical sensor provided comparable quantitative viability assessments to the established colorimetric assay. Besides, the successful discrimination between irritants and non-irritants in both cell types suggests that this platform is for reliable, consistent, and highly predictive cell viability regardless of their origin.

The specific statistical agreement between the electrochemical and optical methods in the chemical exposure panel confirms that the electrochemical readout is equivalent to the industrial gold standard, but with the added benefits of rapid readout and potential for miniaturization.

The most critical finding of this work is the validation of the sensor in RHE models. 3D tissues represent the most challenging matrix for viability assays due to their thickness and opacity. The fact that the electrochemical sensor matched the spectrophotometric results with no statistically significant differences proves that the method is unaffected by the complex tissue architecture. This strong concordance validates the electrochemical capability of the sensor to accurately and reliably assess the viability of complex 3D human skin models,48,49,50,51 providing a robust and ethical alternative for in vitro toxicology and drug safety evaluation in tissue engineering. As demonstrated by the histological analysis in Figure 8, the tissue architecture remains intact post-measurement. This allows for a multi-parametric characterization, enabling researchers to correlate real-time metabolic data with endpoint structural assessments on a single RHE, thereby reducing experimental variability and the number of required tissue models.

By eliminating optical interference, this technology enables the analysis of wider range of compounds, where traditional colorimetric assays often fail or require destructive processing steps. Since the measurement is performed on the culture supernatant, the 3D reconstructed tissue remains functionally and structurally intact. This characteristic is crucial for advanced toxicological studies, as it enables subsequent analyses, such as histology or cytokine quantification, on the same tissue sample, thereby maximizing the data obtained per experiment and reducing the number of models required (Table S1). Moreover, this capability enables the integration of this sensor into automated, high-throughput screening platforms for drug development and safety testing, aligning with the global shift toward animal-free testing methodologies.

In conclusion, this study establishes a robust electrochemical platform for the precise quantification of cell viability in complex in vitro models. By coupling the metabolic specificity of MTS with electrochemical detection, we have successfully eliminated the dependence on optical transparency, overcoming the sensitivity and interference limitations of traditional colorimetric assays. The validation on reconstructed human epidermis (RHE), a challenging, stratified tissue, demonstrates the sensor’s transversal applicability, proving it matches regulatory gold standards while offering superior precision.

However, beyond skin irritation, this technology represents a versatile tool for the broader field of toxicology and drug development. Its ability to function in opaque matrices and its potential for miniaturization make it an ideal candidate for integration into automated, and scalable for high-throughput screening pipelines. Ultimately, this platform provides a reliable, quantifiable solution that supports the global regulatory shift toward animal-free testing, enabling the wider adoption of predictive 3D tissue models in biomedical research.

sources.label: Limitations of the study
sources.text:
Limitations of the study

Although the developed electrochemical platform offers high precision and successfully eliminates optical interferences in RHE models, some constraints remain. The current configuration relies on manual collection of the culture supernatant after a 4-h incubation period with the MTS reagent, meaning it operates as a standardized endpoint evaluation rather than a fully automated, continuous real-time monitoring system. Additionally, while the metabolic principle of the sensor is transversal to all mammalian cells, the system has been validated exclusively within a specific skin toxicity panel and validation in other tissue models could be considered in future studies.

sources.label: Human dermal fibroblast cell cultures
sources.text:
Human dermal fibroblast cell cultures

To perform the different biological assays, commercial human primary dermal fibroblasts (hDFs) (Cat# C-12300, PromoCell, Germany) were used. hDFs were cultured in DMEM, 10% FBS, and 1% Ab/Am at 37°C and 5% CO2. Cell culture medium was changed every 2-3 days, and when 80% confluence was reached, cells were subcultured. All cells were tested for mycoplasma by PCR, and when positive, treated with BIOMYC™-1 and BIOMYC™-2 (Cat# 03-036-1C and Cat# 03-037-1C, respectively, Sartorius AG, Germany) for mycoplasma elimination.
sources.includedScope: JATS sec9.2.1: all direct textual children and tables; nested sections and figures supplied separately. Whitespace normalized; no scientific corrections.

sources.label: N/TERT-1 keratinocyte cell cultures
sources.text:
N/TERT-1 keratinocyte cell cultures

To perform the different biological assays, immortalized N/TERT-1 human keratinocytes (ATCC CVCL_CW92) were used. N/TERT-1 keratinocytes were cultured in serum-free EpiLife supplemented with HKGS and 1% Ab/Am at 37°C and 5% CO2. Culture medium was changed every 2 days and when confluence reached 50-60 % cells were subcultured following protocols from Dickson et al.52 and Régnier et al.53 All cells were tested for mycoplasma by PCR, and when positive, treated with BIOMYC™-1 and BIOMYC™-2 (Cat# 03-036-1C and Cat# 03-037-1C, respectively, Sartorius AG, Germany) for mycoplasma elimination.
sources.includedScope: JATS sec9.2.2: all direct textual children and tables; nested sections and figures supplied separately. Whitespace normalized; no scientific corrections.

sources.label: Reconstructed Human Epidermis cultures
sources.text:
Reconstructed Human Epidermis cultures

To create the RHE, Nunc Cell Culture Inserts in Carrier Plate Systems (0.4 μm pore size) (Cat# 141002, ThermoFisher Scientific) were coated with bovine Collagen I (Cat# C9791, Sigma Aldrich) (0.1 mg/mL) for 1 hour at 37°C, then washed with PBS and air-dried under UV light. NTERT-1 cells were seeded at a concentration of 4,900 cells/mm2. Cells were kept in EpiLife until confluency was reached, and then the inserts were lifted to air-liquid interface (ALI), and culture medium was changed to CnT-Prime 3D Airlift Medium (Cat# CnT-PR-3D, CellnTec): DMEM (60:40) to allow terminal differentiation.54 Media was changed every other day, and the epidermis were kept for 10 days to ensure complete differentiation and cornification, changing media every other day.

sources.label: Electrochemical measurements
sources.text:
Electrochemical measurements

Cyclic voltammetry (CV) response of MTS experiments were performed using a DropSens potentiostat (μStat 300, from Metrohm DropSens, Llanera, Spain) interfaced with DropView 8400 software. All measurements were conducted in a three-electrode configuration using commercial screen-printed carbon electrodes (SPCEs) from Metrohm DropSens (DRP-C110). The electrochemical cell integrated in the strip consisted of a carbon working electrode (WE, 4 mm diameter), a carbon counter electrode (CE), and a silver reference electrode (RE). All potentials reported in this work are referred to this internal Ag reference electrode.

For each experiment, 50 μL of the sample solution was added to the sensor electrode surface, and three consecutive scans were recorded to ensure system stabilization and electrochemical stability of the material. The potential was swept from a starting potential of -0.6 V to a final potential of +0.7 V. The scan rate was set to 50 mV/s. All experiments were performed at room temperature (25°C). After every measurement, the sample was removed and the electrode was washed with Dulbecco′s Phosphate Buffered Saline 1X (Cat# D8537, Sigma Aldrich) and carefully dried with absorbent paper.

Following the cell incubation period with the MTS reagent (see Section MTS assay), the resulting supernatant was collected and measured directly without any prior sample purification or complex pre-processing steps. Furthermore, the screen-printed carbon electrodes (SPCEs) were used without any surface modification or activation.

sources.label: Validation of the MTS electrochemical signal
sources.text:
Validation of the MTS electrochemical signal

Three different culture media, Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM high glucose with GlutaMAX, Cat# D6429, Gibco, ThermoFisher Scientific) supplemented with a 10% Fetal Bovine Serum (FBS, Cat# F7524, Sigma Aldrich) and 1% antibiotic/antimycotic (Ab/Am) (Penicillin-Streptomycin, Cat# P4333, ThermoFisher Scientific); and EpiLife Medium (Cat# MEPI500CA, ThermoFisher Scientific) supplemented with Human Keratinocyte Growth Serum (HKGS, Cat# S0015, ThermoFisher Scientific) and 1% Ab/Am, were tested to evaluate their influence on the electrochemical response of the system with cyclic voltammetry.

To further validate the system, control experiments were conducted with each medium and MTS individually to check for potential interferences. For that purpose, nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NADH, Cat# 10128023001, Roche) was chosen as the reducing agent of MTS at concentrations ranging from 0.005 to 0.1 mg/mL in intervals of 0.005 mg/mL in DMEM and EpiLife.

These measurements were used to obtain a calibration curve for the sensor relating absorbance and signal intensity, providing detection and saturation limits, and assessing its reproducibility. Additionally, extra measurements were performed with non-reduced MTS, and EpiLife or DMEM as blanks, respectively.

The Limit of Detection (LOD) was calculated according to ICH guidelines using the formula LOD = 3.3σ/S, where σ is the standard deviation of the residuals (Sy.x) from the linear regression and S is the slope of the calibration curve.55

sources.label: NADH production inhibition
sources.text:
NADH production inhibition

To evaluate the dependence of the electrochemical signal on cellular metabolism, NADH production was inhibited56 using a specific NADH-oxidase (HY-152026, CAS No.: 2762405-17-2, MedChemExpress). Cells were seeded at a density of 105 cells/mL and allowed to adhere overnight. A 5 mM stock solution was prepared in DMSO, according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Cells were then incubated with varying concentrations of the inhibitor (0.1, 0.5, 1, 2, 5, and 10 μM) for 24 h prior to the MTS assay (described in Section MTS assay section). To account for potential toxic effects, a control group was treated with an equivalent concentration of DMSO, corresponding to equivalent DMSO doses used in the inhibited groups.

sources.label: Histological processing
sources.text:
Histological processing

Skin samples were removed from the culture insert by carefully cutting the membrane using a scalpel, introduced into a histology cassette, and fixed in 10% neutral buffered tissue formalin (Cat# HT501128-4L, Sigma Aldrich) for 2 hours. The samples were then dehydrated in an automated tissue processor (KD-TS1A, Kedee Histology Co.,LTD) for paraffin inclusion. Samples were finally embedded in paraffin blocks, manually cut into 5 μm slices using a microtome (MR 3000, Histo-Line Laboratories), and transferred to microscope slides.

Then, tissue slices were deparaffinized using X-free Solvent for histology xylene substitute (Cat# 06-1305Q, Bio-Optica Milano S.p.A.) and successive dilutions of ethanol (Cat# 1009835000, Supelco) to rehydrate the samples. Hematoxylin & Eosin (H&E, Cat# 05-06013/L and Cat# 05-10009/L, Bio-optical, Labolan) staining was performed following the manufacturer’s protocol and fixed using mounting medium (Cat# 03989-100ML, Eukitt, Sigma-Aldrich).

sources.label: MTS assay
sources.text:
MTS assay

To perform the MTS assay (CellTiter 96 aqueous non-radioactive cell proliferation assay, Cat# G3582, Promega, USA), a solution mixing the specific culture medium of the cell type and 10% of MTS reagent was prepared in the dark. Then, this solution was added to the cells and incubated at 37°C for 4 hours. After incubation, the reduced supernatant was collected and transferred to a 96-well plate (Cat# CLS353075, ThermoFisher Scientific) for measurement. The colorimetric reading was performed by measurement of absorbance in a Synergy™ HTX Multi-Mode Microplate Reader, mixing the samples with an orbital spin of 200 rpm and using a wavelength of 490 nm.

sources.label: Cell confluency and MTS electrochemical signal correlation
sources.text:
Cell confluency and MTS electrochemical signal correlation

To assess the correlation between cell confluency and the measured electrochemical and colorimetric MTS signal, cells were seeded in a 24-well culture plate (Cat# 142475, ThermoFisher Scientific, USA) at increasing confluences from 10% to 100%, based on the cell culture numbers stipulated by the manufacturer. For these specific plates, 100% of confluency corresponds to 240,000 cells, and the remaining cell densities were calculated accordingly, decreasing in 10% increments. The next day, the culture media were removed from the wells and washed with PBS. After that, the MTS assay and electrochemical sensing procedure were performed as explained before (subsection MTS assay section and subsection electrochemical measurements section, respectively).

sources.label: Cell viability assessment after chemical exposure
sources.text:
Cell viability assessment after chemical exposure

For the irritation and corrosion assessment in the RHE models, six reference chemicals, selected based on OECD Test Guideline 439: “Performance Standards for the Assessment of Proposed Similar or Modified in Vitro Reconstructed Human Epidermis (RHE) Test Methods for Skin Irritation Testing”,57,58 were employed: isopropanol (Cat# 190764, Sigma Aldrich), 1-decanol (Cat# 150584-500G, Sigma Aldrich), and 1-bromo-4-chlorobutane (Cat# B60800-25G, Sigma Aldrich). These substances were applied topically in their original form (100% concentration) to simulate direct exposure conditions. Additionally, a 5% aqueous potassium hydroxide (KOH) solution (Cat# 221473-25G, Sigma Aldrich) was used as a severe chemical stressor. Sterile PBS was employed as the negative control, while a 5% aqueous solution of sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS) (Cat# 436143-25G, Sigma Aldrich) served as the validated positive control for the procedure. All liquid solutions were prepared weight/volume (w/v) in deionized water (Table S2).

Six chemicals extracted from the OECD “Performance Standards for the Assessment of Proposed Similar or Modified in Vitro Reconstructed Human Epidermis (RHE) Test Methods for Skin Irritation Testing” as Described in TG 439,57,58 were utilized for this experiment: isopropanol (Cat# 190764, Sigma Aldrich), 5% aqueous potassium hydroxide (KOH) (Cat# 221473-25G, Sigma Aldrich), 1-decanol (Cat# 150584-500G, Sigma Aldrich) and 1-bromo-4-chlorobutane (Cat# B60800-25G, Sigma Aldrich). PBS was used as a negative control, and 5% aqueous solution of sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS Cat# 436143-25G, Sigma Aldrich) as a positive control for the procedure.

To study the effect of these chemicals on the cells, both hDFs and immortalized N/TERT-1 were seeded at confluency in 96-well plates and incubated for 24 hours at 37°C and 5% CO2.

On the experiment day, cell culture media were removed from all the wells, and 50 μL of each of the chemicals was applied to the cells for 60 minutes. After the chemical exposition, samples were washed three times with PBS for 5 minutes each, and then a recovery incubation of 42 hours was carried out in the corresponding cell culture medium.

Afterwards, the MTS assay was carried out, including a sample consisting of culture medium and 10% MTS in order to subtract colorimetric and electrochemical background, as defined in the test guidelines.

Cellular viability was measured according to the OECD Guide stated above. The results obtained for the negative control (PBS) were considered as 100% of cell viability, and the rest of the percentages were extrapolated from this value.

sources.label: Skin irritation assessment after chemical exposure
sources.text:
Skin irritation assessment after chemical exposure

To assess the skin irritation potential of chemicals in a physiologically relevant in vitro model that closely mimics human skin, RHE models were employed. The RHE models were developed using N/TERT-1 keratinocytes as detailed in Section reconstructed human epidermis cultures and were matured until complete differentiation and cornification (10 days at air-liquid interface) to ensure their suitability for irritation testing. This methodology aligns with the principles established in OECD Test Guidelines for in vitro skin irritation (TG 439).57

A panel of six test chemicals (isopropanol, 5% aqueous potassium hydroxide (KOH), 1-decanol, 1-bromo-4-chlorobutane, hydrochloric acid (HCl) (Cat# 258148-25ML, Sigma Aldrich) and 10% sulfuric acid (Cat# 1603151000, Supelco), along with PBS (negative control) and 5% aqueous SDS (positive control), was utilized for RHE exposure.

On the day of the experiment, RHE inserts were carefully transferred, and the culture medium was removed from the wells. A volume of 50 μL of each test chemical was applied directly to the apical surface of the RHE model as a standardized exposure period of 60 minutes. Following chemical exposure, the RHE inserts were thoroughly washed three times with PBS for 5 minutes each to remove residual chemicals. A recovery incubation of 42 hours was then performed adding fresh EpiLife medium to allow for potential cellular recovery.

Subsequently, the viability of the RHE models was quantified using the MTS assay (as described in Section MTS assay section), employing both the electrochemical sensor and conventional colorimetric measurement. Cellular viability for RHE models was measured following the specified OECD Test Guidelines.57 The results obtained for the negative control (PBS) were considered 100% viability, and the rest of the percentages were extrapolated relative to this value.

sources.label: Quantification and statistical analysis
sources.text:
Quantification and statistical analysis

Statistical analysis was performed using GraphPad Prism software v.8.0.2 (GraphPad, Dotmatics, USA). All averages and deviations were subjected to 1-way and 2-way ANOVA tests with a significance value of 0.05 to determine the statistical significance of the results. Errors in the readings were calculated using the standard deviations of each measurement. All experiments were performed with sample replications n = 7 and RHE samples with n = 4. In each figure, the employed test is described in the figure legends. Statistical significance was defined as p < 0.05 (∗), p < 0.01 (∗∗) or p < 0.001 (∗∗∗).

sources.text:
SUPPLEMENTARY MATERIAL
















Figure S1. Schematic representation of the electrochemical MTS cell viability detection
mechanism.
A)  Biological  Context:  Metabolically  active  cells  utilize  mitochondrial  enzymes,  specifically
Succinate Dehydrogenase, as part of the respiratory chain. This activity serves as a direct
indicator  of  cellular  health  and  functional  state.         B)  Molecular  Mechanism:  Mitochondrial
dehydrogenases facilitate the reduction of NAD+ to NADH, generating the intracellular reducing
power required for the assay. C) Chemical Reaction: The exogenously added MTS tetrazolium
salt enters the cellular environment where it is reduced by NADH  to form a highly soluble
formazan product. Unlike other tetrazolium salts, the MTS-formazan is readily released into the
extracellular culture medium, avoiding cell lysis.            D)   Electrochemical Detection: The soluble
formazan is quantified       using Screen-Printed Carbon Electrodes (SPCE). The cathodic peak
current measured at approximately -0.2 V through Cyclic Voltammetry (CV) is proportional to the
concentration of formazan produced, and thus, to the number of viable cells present in the sample.
Illustration created using Canva professional design software (Canva Pty Ltd, Australia).

sources.text:
Figure S2. Electrochemical control and selectivity of the MTS/formazan assay.

Cyclic voltammetry scans were performed                in different conditions to verify the origin of the
electrochemical signal. The absence of redox peaks in these controls confirms that the individual
components do not interfere with the detection window. The characteristic peak is only observed
in the presence of both MTS and NADH, confirming that the sensor specifically quantifies the
reduced MTS product (formazan).



















Figure S3. Calibration curve and sensitivity analysis using Cyclic Voltammetry (CV).
Main plot shows the absolute cathodic peak current (|Ip|) as a function of NADH concentration
over the full experimental range. Inset: Linear regression analysis of the low-concentration regime
(R2 = 0.9516), used for the analytical validation of the sensor. The Limit of Detection (LOD) was
calculated as 3.3 σ /S, where σ represents the standard deviation of the residuals (Sy.x = 0.2292)
and S is the slope of the linear fit. The resulting LOD of 0,0047 mg/mL demonstrates the platform's
capacity to quantify subtle metabolic changes.

Table  S1.    Comparative  analysis  of  analytical  performance  and  operational  features
between  conventional  MTS  colorimetry  and  the  proposed  electrochemical  sensing
platform.

 Feature                        Spectrophotometry (MTS/MTT)                 Proposed      Electrochemical
                                                                            Method

 Optical Interferences          High (Turbidity, pigments)                  None (Redox specific)

 Path-length                    Yes  (Limits  sensitivity  in  small        No (Surface area dependent)
 dependency                     volumes)

 Tissue Preservation            Often requires destructive steps            Fully Non-Destructive

 Scalability                    High (96/384-well plates)                   High         (Multichannel/96-well
                                                                            SPCE)

Note: The comparison highlights the advantages of the electrochemical method in 3D tissue
models (RHE). Optical interference refers to the impact of sample turbidity or endogenous
pigments on signal accuracy. Path-length dependency indicates whether the sensitivity is limited
by the physical volume/depth of the sample (Beer-Lambert law)1. Tissue preservation assesses
the capability to perform secondary analyses (e.g., histology or cytokine profiling) on the same
biological  insert  post-measurement2.  Cost  and  portability  considerations  are  based  on  the
requirements for a standard microplate reader versus a miniaturized, portable potentiostat with
disposable screen-printed electrodes (SPCEs)3.
